claim: miR-1 is a highly conserved microRNA expressed predominantly in C. elegans muscle tissues including pharyngeal muscle, body wall muscle, and sex muscles.
source: mir-1 is a highly conserved microRNA expressed predominantly in C. elegans muscle tissues including pharyngeal muscle, body wall muscle, and sex muscles (Andachi and Kohara, 2016; Martinez et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Andachi and Kohara, 2016; Martinez et al., 2008).

claim: miR-1 expression persists throughout adulthood, declining by half from day 1 to day 14 of adulthood.
source: While microRNAs are known as important developmental regulators (Ivey and Srivastava, 2015), miR-1 expression also persists throughout adulthood, declining by half from day 1 to day 14 of adulthood (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, data from Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and citation to Zhou et al., 2019.

claim: The mir-1(gk276) allele is a 192 base pair deletion that removes the mir-1 coding region as well as the downstream non-coding region.
source: We therefore focused on gk276, a smaller 192 base pair deletion that removes the mir-1 coding region as well as the downstream non-coding region, and used this deletion in our experiments.
evidence: Direct statement about the molecular nature of the gk276 allele.

claim: The mir-1(dh1111) allele deletes a 53 base pair region within the mir-1 locus.
source: We also generated an independent mir-1 allele, dh1111, by CRISPR genome engineering (Figure 1A), which deletes a 53 base pair region within the mir-1 locus.
evidence: Supported by description in text and Figure 1A showing the deletion.

claim: Both mir-1(gk276) and mir-1(dh1111) alleles failed to express the mature miRNA as measured by TaqMan qPCR and are mir-1 null mutants.
source: Both alleles failed to express the mature miRNA as measured by TaqMan qPCR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), and thus are mir-1 null mutants.
evidence: Supported by TaqMan qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: mir-1 mutants (gk276 and dh1111) developed normally and had normal brood size.
source: We found that mir-1 mutants gk276 and dh1111 developed normally, had normal brood size, and near normal life span (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: mir-1 mutants have near normal life span.
source: We found that mir-1 mutants gk276 and dh1111 developed normally, had normal brood size, and near normal life span (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Supported by life span data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: Motility on solid media, thrashing in liquid medium, and pharyngeal pumping ability at days 8 and 14 of adulthood were similar to N2 wild-type controls in mir-1 mutants.
source: Additionally, motility on solid media, thrashing in liquid medium, and pharyngeal pumping ability determined at days 8 and 14 of adulthood were similar to N2 wild-type (WT) controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G and Supplementary file 1b.

claim: mir-1 deletion showed little distinction from WT with moderate heat stress by growth at 25°C.
source: We saw little distinction from WT with moderate heat stress by growth at 25°C nor heat shock resistance at 35°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, H, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, H and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: mir-1 deletion showed little distinction from WT with heat shock resistance at 35°C.
source: We saw little distinction from WT with moderate heat stress by growth at 25°C nor heat shock resistance at 35°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, H, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, H and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: mir-1 mutants displayed significantly less polyQ35 aggregates (avg. 38 and 36, day 4 of adulthood) compared to age-matched WT controls (avg. 53).
source: Interestingly, we observed that mir-1 mutants displayed significantly less aggregates (avg. 38 and 36, day 4 of adulthood) compared to age-matched WT controls (avg. 53) at this time (Figure 1B, C, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1B, C and Supplementary file 1b.

claim: About 30% of the mir-1;Q35 mutants left the circle while only 2.5% of the control Q35 worms did so in the circle test on day 8 of adulthood.
source: We observed that about 30% of the mir-1;Q35 mutants left the circle while only 2.5% of the control Q35 worms did so (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Supported by motility data shown in Figure 1D and Supplementary file 1b.

claim: Both mir-1 mutants gk276 and dh1111 were significantly more mobile (avg. 16, 15 body bends) compared to age-matched Q35 controls (avg. two body bends) in the thrashing assay on day 8 of adulthood.
source: Though the degree of paralysis was more variable, both mir-1 mutants gk276 and dh1111 were significantly more mobile (avg. 16, 15 body bends) compared to age-matched Q35 controls (avg. two body bends, Figure 1E, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Supported by thrashing assay data shown in Figure 1E and Supplementary file 1b.

claim: mir-1(gk276) mutants did significantly better than WT for several measures of activity (activity index, brush stroke, travel speed, wave initiation rate) and gait (number of body waves) on day 8 in the presence of Q35.
source: In the presence of Q35, however, mir-1(gk276) mutants did significantly better than WT for several measures of activity (activity index, brush stroke, travel speed, wave initiation rate) and gait (number of body waves) on day 8 (Figure 1F–H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I–M, Supplementary file 1c), consistent with the idea that mir-1 mutation protects against Q35 proteotoxic stress during mid-life.
evidence: Supported by CeleST analysis data shown in Figure 1F–H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I–M, and Supplementary file 1c.

claim: The pumping rate of mir-1;Q35 worms was significantly increased (gk276, avg. 60; dh1111, avg. 78) compared to Q35 controls (avg. 16) on day 8 of adulthood.
source: We observed that the pumping rate of mir-1;Q35 worms was significantly increased (gk276, avg. 60; dh1111, avg. 78) compared to Q35 controls (avg. 16) on day 8 of adulthood (Figure 1L, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Supported by pharyngeal pumping data shown in Figure 1L and Supplementary file 1b.

claim: The life span of mir-1(dh1111);Q35 strains was significantly extended (n = 3, mean 13 [WT] vs. 19 [dh1111] days) compared to Q35 alone.
source: Furthermore, we found that the life span of mir-1(dh1111);Q35 strains was significantly extended (n = 3, mean 13 [WT] vs. 19 [dh1111] days) compared to Q35 alone (Figure 1J, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Supported by life span data shown in Figure 1J and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: Introducing a WT mir-1 transgene into the mir-1(gk276) background restored normal levels of mature miR-1.
source: Introducing a WT mir-1 transgene into the mir-1(gk276) background restored normal levels of mature miR-1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1N) and largely reversed mir-1 phenotypes, showing increased Q35 aggregates, decreased motility, pumping rate, and life span compared to non-transgenic controls (Figure 1K–O, Supplementary file 1a, b).
evidence: Supported by TaqMan qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1N.

claim: The WT mir-1 transgene largely reversed mir-1 phenotypes, showing increased Q35 aggregates, decreased motility, pumping rate, and life span compared to non-transgenic controls.
source: Introducing a WT mir-1 transgene into the mir-1(gk276) background restored normal levels of mature miR-1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1N) and largely reversed mir-1 phenotypes, showing increased Q35 aggregates, decreased motility, pumping rate, and life span compared to non-transgenic controls (Figure 1K–O, Supplementary file 1a, b).
evidence: Supported by rescue data shown in Figure 1K–O, Supplementary file 1a, b.

claim: Aggregate numbers were significantly reduced in mir-1(gk276);Q40 L4 worms.
source: We found aggregate numbers significantly reduced in mir-1(gk276);Q40 L4 worms (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Supported by data in Supplementary file 1b.

claim: The motility of mir-1(gk276);Q40 worms was unaffected at day 3 of adulthood and reduced in two out of three experiments at day 7 of adulthood compared to Q40 controls.
source: However, the motility of mir-1(gk276);Q40 worms, determined by 1 min thrashing assays, was unaffected at day 3 of adulthood and reduced in two out of three experiments at day 7 of adulthood compared to Q40 controls (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Supported by motility data in Supplementary file 1b.

claim: Aggregate numbers were reduced in mir-1(gk276);α-syn worms at day 1 of adulthood compared to the α-syn control.
source: Similarly, aggregate numbers were reduced in mir-1(gk276);α-syn worms at day 1 of adulthood compared to the α-syn control (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Supported by data in Supplementary file 1b.

claim: Thrashing of mir-1(gk276);α-syn worms was significantly reduced on day 1 of adulthood, but by day 5 there was no significant difference in motility between mir-1(gk276);α-syn and α-syn worms.
source: Thrashing of mir-1(gk276);α-syn worms was significantly reduced on day 1 of adulthood, but by day 5 there was no significant difference in motility between mir-1(gk276);α-syn and α-syn worms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1O, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Supported by thrashing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1O and Supplementary file 1b.

claim: mir-1 loss reduced aggregate numbers in three different proteotoxic stress paradigms (polyQ35, polyQ40, and α-synuclein).
source: Taken together, mir-1 loss reduced aggregate numbers in three different proteotoxic stress paradigms.
evidence: Summary statement based on data from multiple proteotoxic models.

claim: Reduced number of aggregates did not always directly correlate with improved motility.
source: However, reduced number of aggregates did not always directly correlate with improved motility, reinforcing the notion that protein aggregation may promote or aggravate health depending on the proteotoxic species and age (Cohen et al., 2006).
evidence: Inference from experimental observations across different proteotoxic models, supported by citation to Cohen et al., 2006.

claim: Computational prediction tools identified 68 overlapping candidate miR-1 targets.
source: This yielded 68 overlapping candidates (Figure 2A; Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1d.

claim: Network analysis of 68 predicted miR-1 targets revealed a tight cluster of predicted targets encoding 11/21 subunits of the vacuolar ATPase.
source: Interestingly, network analysis of these 68 genes using STRING (string-db.org) (Snel et al., 2000) revealed a tight cluster of predicted targets encoding 11/21 subunits of the vacuolar ATPase (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by STRING network analysis shown in Figure 2B and citation to Snel et al., 2000.

claim: Five additional vacuolar ATPase genes were identified by two of the three prediction algorithms.
source: Five additional vacuolar ATPase genes were identified by two of the three prediction algorithms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: daf-16/FOXO and hlh-30/TFEB genes contain predicted miR-1 binding sites in their 3′UTRs.
source: In addition, two genes that code transcription factors implicated in lysosome biogenesis, daf-16/FOXO and hlh-30/TFEB (Sardiello et al., 2009; Settembre et al., 2011), also contained predicted miR-1 binding sites in their 3′UTRs.
evidence: Supported by computational prediction and citations to Sardiello et al., 2009 and Settembre et al., 2011.

claim: Vacuolar ATPase subunits vha-1, vha-8, vha-9, vha-13, and vha-14, as well as muscle gene zyx-1, stood out as molecules suppressing mir-1 motility in the RNAi screen.
source: Among the selected candidates, vacuolar ATPase subunits vha-1, vha-8, vha-9, vha-13, and vha-14, as well as muscle gene zyx-1, stood out as molecules suppressing mir-1 motility (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by RNAi screen data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: TMT shotgun proteomic analysis identified approximately 1500–2000 proteins in the replicates comparing mir-1 mutants to WT worms on day 1 of adulthood.
source: We identified approximately 1500–2000 proteins in the replicates (Figure 2D, Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: Supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 2D and Supplementary file 1f.

claim: Proteomic samples showed a high degree of correlation with minimal separation of WT and mir-1 genotypes.
source: Samples showed a high degree of correlation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) with minimal separation of WT and mir-1 genotypes, reflecting the subtle changes induced by mir-1 mutation at the organismal level.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: v-ATPase subunits vha-1, vha-9, vha-13, vha-14, and vha-19 were confirmed as likely mediators of mir-1;Q35 motility in the thrashing assay.
source: Based on the prominence of v-ATPase genes among both the informatic and the proteomic candidates, we systematically tested 10 of them in the thrashing assay, confirming v-ATPase subunits vha-1, vha-9, vha-13, vha-14, and vha-19 as likely mediators of mir-1;Q35 motility (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by thrashing assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: vha-13 RNAi significantly reduced motility of mir-1;Q35 strains in the circle test and thrashing assays.
source: We further tested the impact of vha-5 and vha-13 on mir-1;Q35 phenotypes in more detail, as well as transcription factors daf-16/FOXO and hlh-30/TFEB as potential miR-1 targets that mediate lysosomal biogenesis. Using the circle test, thrashing assay, and pharyngeal pumping as readout (Figure 2F–H), we again verified in particular the role of vha-13 in reducing mir-1 motility.
evidence: Supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 2F–H.

claim: daf-16/FOXO and hlh-30/TFEB RNAi reduced motility as measured in the circle test, indicating a potential requirement for these transcription factors.
source: In addition, daf-16/FOXO and hlh-30/TFEB RNAi reduced motility as measured in the circle test, indicating a potential requirement for these transcription factors.
evidence: Supported by circle test data.

claim: The effect on motility was specific to the mir-1 background for vha-5, vha-13, and hlh-30 since RNAi of these genes had no significant effect on motility in N2;Q35 worms.
source: We also confirmed that the effect on motility was specific to the mir-1 background for vha-5, vha-13, and hlh-30 since RNAi of these genes had no significant effect on motility in N2;Q35 worms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by counter-screen data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The mRNA levels of vha-5, vha-10, vha-13, and vha-19, as well as transcription factors hlh-30/TFEB and daf-16/FOXO, were increased approximately twofold in mir-1 mutants compared to age-matched WT worms on day 4 of adulthood.
source: We found that the mRNA levels of vha-5, vha-10, vha-13, and vha-19, as well as transcription factors hlh-30/TFEB and daf-16/FOXO, were increased approximately twofold in mir-1 mutants compared to age-matched WT worms (Figure 3A), consistent with the idea that these genes are miR-1 targets.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 3xFlag::mNeonGreen::vha-13 was strongly expressed in the excretory cell, canal, hypodermis, as well as gut.
source: The 3xFlag::mNeonGreen::vha-13 was strongly expressed in the excretory cell, canal, hypodermis, as well as gut (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by expression pattern shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 3xFlag::mNeonGreen::VHA-13 was localized in discrete foci in the hypodermis.
source: In the hypodermis, 3xFlag::mNeonGreen::VHA-13 was localized in discrete foci (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: 3xFlag::mNeonGreen::VHA-13 resided in miR-1-expressing tissues of body wall muscle, sex muscles, and pharynx, where it was more weakly expressed.
source: Notably, 3xFlag::mNeonGreen::VHA-13 also resided in miR-1-expressing tissues of body wall muscle, sex muscles, and pharynx, where it was more weakly expressed.
evidence: Direct observation of expression pattern.

claim: Within muscle cells, VHA-13 localized to dense bodies (analogous to vertebrate Z disks) and intervening cytosol.
source: Within muscle cells, VHA-13 localized to dense bodies (analogous to vertebrate Z disks) and intervening cytosol (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: vha-13 levels were upregulated in the pharyngeal isthmus of mir-1(gk276) mutants.
source: Strikingly, we observed that vha-13 levels were upregulated in the pharyngeal isthmus of mir-1(gk276) mutants (Figure 3C, D, Supplementary file 1g), while conversely, overexpression of the mir-1 transgene decreased levels in this tissue relative to WT (Figure 3E, Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence quantification shown in Figure 3C, D, and Supplementary file 1g.

claim: Overexpression of the mir-1 transgene decreased vha-13 levels in the pharyngeal isthmus relative to WT.
source: Strikingly, we observed that vha-13 levels were upregulated in the pharyngeal isthmus of mir-1(gk276) mutants (Figure 3C, D, Supplementary file 1g), while conversely, overexpression of the mir-1 transgene decreased levels in this tissue relative to WT (Figure 3E, Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence quantification shown in Figure 3E and Supplementary file 1g.

claim: Mutating both miR-1 binding sites (BS1,2: MUT2) de-repressed VHA-13 levels in the isthmus in the WT background.
source: Mutating both miR-1 binding sites (BS1,2: MUT2), however, de-repressed VHA-13 levels in the isthmus in the WT background (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence quantification shown in Figure 3G.

claim: In double mutants containing both mir-1(gk276) and vha-13 BS1,2 mutations, no clear regulation of vha-13 expression was observed compared to the BS1,2 mutations alone.
source: In double mutants containing both mir-1(gk276) and vha-13 BS1,2 mutations, no clear regulation of vha-13 expression was observed compared to the BS1,2 mutations alone (Figure 3G), suggesting that miR-1 modulates pharyngeal vha-13 expression through both potential miR-1 binding sites.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence quantification shown in Figure 3G.

claim: vha-13 protein levels in the body wall muscle were upregulated in mir-1 mutants compared to WT, as measured by western blots.
source: Consistent with results seen in pharyngeal muscle, vha-13 protein levels in the body wall muscle were also upregulated in mir-1 mutants compared to WT, as measured by western blots (Figure 3H, I).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3H, I.

claim: Exchanging the vha-13 3′UTR with the unc-54 3′UTR lacking miR-1 binding sites blunted regulation by miR-1.
source: Exchanging the vha-13 3′UTR with the unc-54 3′UTR lacking miR-1 binding sites (vha-13::unc-54 3′UTR) blunted regulation by miR-1 (Figure 3F, I), indicating that vha-13 is repressed by miR-1 via its 3′UTR in both body wall and pharyngeal muscle.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3F, I.

claim: Overexpressing vha-13 in the muscle of Q35 worms significantly reduced aggregate number.
source: In accord with this idea, overexpressing vha-13 in the muscle of Q35 worms significantly reduced aggregate number, improved motility, and enhanced pharyngeal pumping ability (Figure 3J–L, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Supported by aggregate quantification shown in Figure 3J and Supplementary file 1b.

claim: Overexpressing vha-13 in the muscle of Q35 worms improved motility.
source: In accord with this idea, overexpressing vha-13 in the muscle of Q35 worms significantly reduced aggregate number, improved motility, and enhanced pharyngeal pumping ability (Figure 3J–L, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Supported by motility data shown in Figure 3K and Supplementary file 1b.

claim: Overexpressing vha-13 in the muscle of Q35 worms enhanced pharyngeal pumping ability.
source: In accord with this idea, overexpressing vha-13 in the muscle of Q35 worms significantly reduced aggregate number, improved motility, and enhanced pharyngeal pumping ability (Figure 3J–L, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Supported by pharyngeal pumping data shown in Figure 3L and Supplementary file 1b.

claim: Overexpressing vha-13 significantly increased the life span of Q35 animals compared to non-transgenic controls in two out of five experiments.
source: It also significantly increased the life span of Q35 animals compared to non-transgenic controls in two out of five experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Supported by life span data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: In muscle-specific miR-1/133a double knockout mice, Atp6v1a/vha-13 and Atp6v1h/vha-15 are significantly upregulated by 2.6-fold and 2.1-fold, respectively.
source: In muscle-specific miR-1/133a double knockout mice, Atp6v1a/vha-13 and Atp6v1h/vha-15 are significantly upregulated by 2.6-fold and 2.1-fold, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by transcriptome data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H from Wüst et al., 2018.

claim: In miR-1-1/miR-1-2 double knockout mice, Atp6v1a/vha-13 is significantly upregulated by 1.49-fold.
source: In miR-1-1/miR-1-2 double knockout mice, Atp6v1a/vha-13 is significantly upregulated by 1.49-fold (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by transcriptome data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I from Wei et al., 2014.

claim: miR-1-dependent regulation of vha-13/Atp6v1a may be conserved during evolution.
source: These findings suggest that miR-1-dependent regulation of vha-13/Atp6v1a may be conserved during evolution.
evidence: Inference based on data from both C. elegans and mouse models.

claim: LMP-1 protein levels were significantly increased in mir-1 mutants compared to WT control, as measured by western blot analysis.
source: LMP-1 protein levels were significantly increased in mir-1 mutants compared to WT control, as measured by western blot analysis (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4C, D.

claim: An increase in the number of acidified puncta was observed in mir-1 mutants at day 4 of adulthood using Lysotracker Red.
source: Using Lysotracker Red, a dye that targets acidic membranous structures such as lysosomes (Chazotte, 2011), we observed an increase in the number of acidified puncta in mir-1 mutants at day 4 of adulthood (Figure 4E, F).
evidence: Supported by Lysotracker staining data shown in Figure 4E, F and citation to Chazotte, 2011.

claim: mir-1 mutation prevents aggregate formation and increases organismal motility and pharyngeal contractility during aging under polyQ35 proteotoxic challenge.
source: Surprisingly, we found that under polyQ35 proteotoxic challenge, mir-1 mutation prevents aggregate formation and increases organismal motility and pharyngeal contractility during aging.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from multiple assays.

claim: miR-1 regulates expression of several lysosomal v-ATPase subunits.
source: Mechanistically, miR-1 regulates expression of several lysosomal v-ATPase subunits and targets a crucial regulatory component, vha-13/ATP6V1A, via its 3′UTR to impact proteotoxicity and longevity.
evidence: Summary of mechanistic findings from multiple experiments.

claim: miR-1 targets vha-13/ATP6V1A via its 3′UTR to impact proteotoxicity and longevity.
source: Mechanistically, miR-1 regulates expression of several lysosomal v-ATPase subunits and targets a crucial regulatory component, vha-13/ATP6V1A, via its 3′UTR to impact proteotoxicity and longevity.
evidence: Supported by 3′UTR mutation experiments and functional assays.

claim: miR-1 regulates lysosomal acidification.
source: Further, miR-1 regulates lysosomal acidification and nuclear localization of HLH-30/TFEB, a key regulator of lysosome biogenesis.
evidence: Supported by Lysotracker staining experiments.

claim: miR-1 regulates nuclear localization of HLH-30/TFEB.
source: Further, miR-1 regulates lysosomal acidification and nuclear localization of HLH-30/TFEB, a key regulator of lysosome biogenesis.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data showing HLH-30 nuclear localization.

claim: miR-1 coordinately regulates lysosomal v-ATPase and biogenesis to impact muscle function and health during aging.
source: Our studies reveal that miR-1 coordinately regulates lysosomal v-ATPase and biogenesis to impact muscle function and health during aging.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on all experimental findings.

claim: Muscle frailty is a hallmark of tissue aging seen in species as diverse as worms, flies, mice, and humans.
source: In fact, muscle frailty is a hallmark of tissue aging seen in species as diverse as worms, flies, mice, and humans (Cruz-Jentoft et al., 2010; Demontis et al., 2013; Herndon et al., 2002; Martinez et al., 2007; Miller et al., 2008; Nair, 2005).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Muscle can respond positively to exercise and stress and rejuvenate even into older age, showing remarkable plasticity.
source: Nevertheless, muscle can respond positively to exercise and stress and rejuvenate even into older age, showing remarkable plasticity (Cartee et al., 2016; Distefano and Goodpaster, 2018; Pollock et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: microRNAs are small 22–26 nucleotide RNAs that bind with complementarity through their seed sequence to target mRNAs to downregulate gene expression.
source: microRNAs are small 22–26 nucleotide RNAs that bind with complementarity through their seed sequence to target mRNAs to downregulate gene expression (Gu and Kay, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gu and Kay, 2010.

claim: Many microRNAs are expressed in a tissue-specific manner and regulate programs cell autonomously.
source: Many microRNAs are expressed in a tissue-specific manner and regulate programs cell autonomously, and could therefore potentially serve as tissue-specific therapeutic targets (Guo et al., 2015; Panwar et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guo et al., 2015 and Panwar et al., 2017.

claim: Some microRNAs are found circulating in serum, raising the possibility that they can act cell non-autonomously.
source: In addition, some microRNAs are found circulating in serum (Chen et al., 2008; Weber et al., 2010), raising the possibility that they can act cell non-autonomously as well.
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2008 and Weber et al., 2010.

claim: miR-1 homologs are muscle-enriched microRNAs that are highly conserved in evolution and important for mammalian heart and muscle development.
source: miR-1 homologs are muscle-enriched microRNAs that are highly conserved in evolution and important for mammalian heart and muscle development (Zhao et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2007.

claim: C. elegans mir-1 deletion mutants are viable and exhibit modest changes in the behavior of the neuromuscular junction.
source: Deletion mutants are viable and exhibit modest changes in the behavior of the neuromuscular junction (Simon et al., 2008) and autophagy (Nehammer et al., 2019), but little else is known of its normative function.
evidence: Supported by citations to Simon et al., 2008 and Nehammer et al., 2019.

claim: C. elegans mir-1 deletion mutants exhibit modest changes in autophagy.
source: Deletion mutants are viable and exhibit modest changes in the behavior of the neuromuscular junction (Simon et al., 2008) and autophagy (Nehammer et al., 2019), but little else is known of its normative function.
evidence: Supported by citation to Nehammer et al., 2019.

claim: The v-ATPase is a multisubunit enzyme that acidifies the endolysosomal lumen to control a plethora of cellular activities.
source: The v-ATPase is a multisubunit enzyme that acidifies the endolysosomal lumen to control a plethora of cellular activities.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about v-ATPase function.

claim: Acidification regulates protein trafficking, endocytic recycling, synaptic vesicle loading, and autophagy, as well as the activity of multiple acid hydrolases and nutrient and ion transporters.
source: Acidification regulates protein trafficking, endocytic recycling, synaptic vesicle loading, and autophagy, as well as the activity of multiple acid hydrolases and nutrient and ion transporters.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about lysosomal acidification functions.

claim: The v-ATPase itself serves as a docking site for regulating mTOR and AMPK complexes and affects metabolism.
source: Moreover, the v-ATPase itself serves as a docking site for regulating mTOR and AMPK complexes and affects metabolism (Settembre et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Settembre et al., 2013 and Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: In mammalian cardiomyocytes, lipid loading inhibits the v-ATPase, leading to a decline in contractile function that could contribute to muscle deficits in diabetes.
source: In mammalian cardiomyocytes, lipid loading inhibits the v-ATPase, leading to a decline in contractile function that could contribute to muscle deficits in diabetes (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2020.

claim: Lesions in VMA21 that disrupt v-ATPase assembly have been shown to cause myopathies.
source: Lesions in VMA21 that disrupt v-ATPase assembly have also been shown to cause myopathies (Dowling et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dowling et al., 2015.

claim: A global increase in levels of lysosomal LMP-1::GFP was observed in western blots in mir-1 mutants.
source: Surprisingly we also found that some mir-1 phenotypes were not strictly limited to muscle since we observed a global increase in levels of lysosomal LMP-1::GFP in western blots, increased lysosomal acidification in the intestine, as well as enhanced nuclear localization of HLH-30/TFEB in the hypodermis.
evidence: Supported by western blot data.

claim: Increased lysosomal acidification in the intestine was observed in mir-1 mutants.
source: Surprisingly we also found that some mir-1 phenotypes were not strictly limited to muscle since we observed a global increase in levels of lysosomal LMP-1::GFP in western blots, increased lysosomal acidification in the intestine, as well as enhanced nuclear localization of HLH-30/TFEB in the hypodermis.
evidence: Supported by Lysotracker staining data.

claim: Enhanced nuclear localization of HLH-30/TFEB in the hypodermis was observed in mir-1 mutants.
source: Surprisingly we also found that some mir-1 phenotypes were not strictly limited to muscle since we observed a global increase in levels of lysosomal LMP-1::GFP in western blots, increased lysosomal acidification in the intestine, as well as enhanced nuclear localization of HLH-30/TFEB in the hypodermis.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data.

claim: miR-1 could act cell non-autonomously, regulating lysosomal biogenesis and associated activities.
source: Given that mir-1 is muscle-expressed, this observation could suggest cell non-autonomous regulation of lysosomal biogenesis and associated activities by miR-1, acting either directly or indirectly.
evidence: Inference based on observation of effects in non-muscle tissues.

claim: In mammals, miR-1 has been identified as a circulating microRNA found in serum exosomes upon exercise stress or cardiac infarction.
source: In mammals, miR-1 has been identified as a circulating microRNA found in serum exosomes upon exercise stress or cardiac infarction, suggesting that it could act systemically (Cheng et al., 2019; D'Souza et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cheng et al., 2019 and D'Souza et al., 2018.

claim: The v-ATPase itself is implicated in exosomal activity.
source: In this light, it is intriguing that the v-ATPase itself is implicated in exosomal activity (Liégeois et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liégeois et al., 2006.

claim: In mammals, miR-1 and its homolog miR-133 are essential to cardiac development and function.
source: In mammals, miR-1 and its homolog miR-133 are essential to cardiac development and function, where they have been shown to regulate Notch ligand Dll1, the GTPase dynamin 2 (DNM2), Frizzled-7 (FZD7), and fibroblast growth factor receptor substrate 2 (FRS2) as targets (Ivey et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2011; Mitchelson and Qin, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ivey et al., 2008, Liu et al., 2011, and Mitchelson and Qin, 2015.

claim: Knockout of mammalian mir1/mir133 specifically in muscle has little overt effect on muscle structure, but rather regulates the developmental transition from glycolytic to oxidative metabolism via the Mef2/Dlk1-Dio3 axis, affecting running endurance.
source: Surprisingly knockout of mammalian mir1/mir133 specifically in muscle has little overt effect on muscle structure, but rather regulates the developmental transition from glycolytic to oxidative metabolism via the Mef2/Dlk1-Dio3 axis, affecting running endurance (Wüst et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wüst et al., 2018.

claim: C. elegans miR-1 regulates mef-2, affecting retrograde signaling at the neuromuscular junction.
source: Similarly, C. elegans miR-1 regulates mef-2, in this case affecting retrograde signaling at the neuromuscular junction (Simon et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Simon et al., 2008.

claim: Most microRNA knockouts do not lead to observable phenotypes in C. elegans.
source: Indeed, most microRNA knockouts do not lead to observable phenotypes in C. elegans (Miska et al., 2007), suggesting that microRNAs often work redundantly or in response to stress to fine-tune gene expression.
evidence: Supported by citation to Miska et al., 2007.

claim: Pocock and colleagues reported that miR-1 downregulates the Rab GTPase TBC-7/TBC1D15, thereby promoting autophagic flux in worms and human cells.
source: Recently, Pocock and colleagues reported that miR-1 downregulates the Rab GTPase TBC-7/TBC1D15, thereby promoting autophagic flux in worms and human cells (Nehammer et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nehammer et al., 2019.

claim: Mammalian studies suggest context-dependent mir-1 effects, where mir-1 either promotes or inhibits autophagy.
source: Mammalian studies suggest context-dependent mir-1 effects, where mir-1 either promotes or inhibits autophagy (Ejlerskov et al., 2020; Hua et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ejlerskov et al., 2020, Hua et al., 2018, and Xu et al., 2020.

claim: DAF-16/FOXO and HLH-30/TFEB regulate lysosome biogenesis, proteostasis, and metabolism, and act in insulin/IGF and mTOR signaling pathways.
source: Among the putative miR-1 targets that we identified in C. elegans are the pro-longevity transcription factors DAF-16/FOXO and HLH-30/TFEB, which regulate lysosome biogenesis, proteostasis, and metabolism, and act in insulin/IGF and mTOR signaling pathways (Lin et al., 2018; O'Rourke and Ruvkun, 2013; Settembre et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lin et al., 2018, O'Rourke and Ruvkun, 2013, and Settembre et al., 2011.

claim: mir-1 mutation led to an upregulation of daf-16 and hlh-30 mRNA during adulthood.
source: mir-1 mutation led to an upregulation of their mRNA during adulthood and enhanced nuclear localization of HLH-30.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data.

claim: mir-1 mutation enhanced nuclear localization of HLH-30.
source: mir-1 mutation led to an upregulation of their mRNA during adulthood and enhanced nuclear localization of HLH-30.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data.

claim: miR-1-predicted targets include pro-aging components of mTOR signaling such as let-363/mTOR and raga-1/RagA.
source: Notably, miR-1-predicted targets also include pro-aging components of mTOR signaling such as let-363/mTOR and raga-1/RagA (targetscan.org), which also regulate the activity or localization of these transcription factors.
evidence: Supported by computational prediction from targetscan.org.

claim: VHA-13/ATP6V1A subunit has been shown to regulate mTOR lysosomal recruitment and activity.
source: Interestingly, VHA-13/ATP6V1A subunit has been shown to regulate mTOR lysosomal recruitment and activity (Chung et al., 2019) and mTOR signaling regulates the activity of TFEB at the lysosomal surface (Settembre et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chung et al., 2019.

claim: mTOR signaling regulates the activity of TFEB at the lysosomal surface.
source: Interestingly, VHA-13/ATP6V1A subunit has been shown to regulate mTOR lysosomal recruitment and activity (Chung et al., 2019) and mTOR signaling regulates the activity of TFEB at the lysosomal surface (Settembre et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Settembre et al., 2013.

claim: Upregulation of v-ATPase activity is associated with the clearance of oxidized protein and rejuvenation of the C. elegans germline.
source: Upregulation of v-ATPase activity is also associated with the clearance of oxidized protein and rejuvenation of the C. elegans germline (Bohnert and Kenyon, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bohnert and Kenyon, 2017.
